text:
WHAT THEY ARE SAYING: Send the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to President Trump’s Desk

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

"Last night, landmark permitting reform legislation passed the Senate. It's one of the biggest things that you will see. It's a big deal… It’s projected to put at least $1,300 a year back in the pockets of hardworking Americans.” – President Donald J. Trump

President Donald J. Trump is committed to fixing America’s broken permitting system standing behind (BAAJA), legislation that will modernize federal environmental reviews and permitting while delivering cheaper energy, high-paying jobs, and economic growth across the United States.

Last night, the Senate advanced landmark permitting reform legislation, and now the House has the opportunity to finish the job and send the bill to President Trump’s desk to lock in generations of affordability and energy dominance for the American people.

Here’s what they’re saying about the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act:

American Exploration & Production Council CEO Anne Bradbury: “AXPC applauds the Senate for taking decisive bipartisan action to remove longstanding barriers to American energy and infrastructure development. BAAJA offers a generational opportunity to cut through permitting delays and lower costs across America without compromising critical environmental protections. With meaningful relief for American families within reach, we respectfully urge the House to send BAAJA to the President’s desk before the end of the year.”

American Chemistry Council: “Yesterday’s vote represents an important step toward addressing longstanding permitting challenges that have delayed projects, increased costs, and hindered economic growth. As demand for energy, advanced manufacturing, and critical infrastructure continues to grow, the United States needs a permitting system capable of supporting investment and development at the speed required to compete globally.

“The future of American manufacturing, infrastructure, and energy development depends on our nation's ability to build. Enactment of this legislation would help ensure the United States remains the best place in the world to invest, manufacture, and innovate “

American Petroleum Institute President and CEO Mike Sommers: “Today’s bipartisan Senate vote marks a major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms that would deliver more affordable energy for consumers, cut costly delays, and build much-needed critical infrastructure. We thank Senators Capito, Lee, Whitehouse and Heinrich for advancing long-overdue reforms.”

Association of American Railroads CEO and President Ian Jefferies: “Senate passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is an encouraging step toward a permitting process that works better for communities and the projects they depend on. Freight railroads make long-term investments in the network that connects businesses, farms, ports, and consumers. When reviews take years, needed improvements can be delayed. This bipartisan legislation can help make project reviews timelier and more predictable while preserving important environmental protections.”

Business Roundtable CEO Joshua Bolten: “Business Roundtable applauds the Senate for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. The strong bipartisan vote marks an important step toward enacting comprehensive permitting reforms that would help lower costs for American families and businesses.

“By modernizing the federal permitting system, this legislation would make it easier to build critical energy projects, roads, ports and other much-needed infrastructure. The benefits would flow to Americans in the form of lower utility bills, new good-paying jobs and more private-sector investment in communities across the country. We urge the House to finish the job and swiftly pass this measure.”

Interstate Natural Gas Association of America President and CEO Amy Andryszak: “Tonight’s Senate vote marks a pivotal step toward modernizing America’s permitting process and ensuring affordable energy for American consumers. Enshrining improvements to the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), judicial reviews, and permit certainty in statute will help accelerate the buildout of the critical energy infrastructure needed to meet growing demand and ensure a reliable, affordable energy future.

“We applaud Senators for reaching bipartisan consensus and urge the U.S. House of Representatives to act quickly to send this legislation to the President’s desk. The House must pass this legislation without further delay to help meet America’s energy needs and address rising energy costs.”

Laborers International Union of North America President Brent Booker: “For more than a decade, endless permitting delays have stalled critical infrastructure projects that put our members to work across the country. Every month a project sits on the shelf, LIUNA members go without paychecks. This bill ends the runaround. It sets clear timelines and holds the process accountable, so projects get decided and built. Congress has spent years talking about the need to fix our broken permitting process. Now it has a real opportunity to do something about it. The cost of inaction is too high: lost jobs, lost investment, and lost opportunities for working Americans. We cannot afford to let another Congress come and go while critical projects remain stalled and working families pay the price.”

National Association of Home Builders: “With so many families priced out of the market, the House must pass this bill without delay. BAAJA will make federal permits faster and less costly for builders and developers, lowering land development costs and making lots more affordable. It also helps multifamily developers by ensuring that the use of federal grants and loans does not automatically trigger a National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review. For projects that still need a NEPA review, the bill sets enforceable deadlines for agencies to complete it.”

National Electrical Manufacturers Association President and CEO Debra Phillips: “America’s electricity needs are growing rapidly, and this legislation will help us build the infrastructure to meet them. It speeds up transmission projects, encourages grid-enhancing advanced transmission technologies, and gives investors more certainty, which means more reliable, affordable power for consumers. That will help America build the energy system our future demands, and move past an outdated permitting system that has been tangled in red tape for too long. We commend the bipartisan leadership that made this progress possible and urge the House to finish the job.”

National Mining Association President and CEO Rich Nolan: “We’re grateful to the Senate for coming together to move legislation that will help transform American potential into American production, and for the leadership of Senators Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich, who deserve great credit for their tireless work to advance the bill. True economic and national security comes with a United States that can build things again, using domestic materials and domestic fuels, and decisively confront China’s supply chain dominance. It’s now up to the House to say American prosperity and competitiveness matter, ensure that made in America can also be mined in America, and pass this legislation.”

National Rural Electric Cooperative Association CEO Jim Matheson: “This legislation will dramatically improve the federal permitting system, making it more manageable and predictable for electric co-ops as they work to keep the lights on at a cost families and businesses can afford. Today’s environmental review processes can take years, delaying critical energy projects and increasing costs that ultimately fall on consumers. The bill will streamline reviews and reduce litigation delays, while leaving important environmental protections in place.”

U.S. Oil and Gas Association President Tim Stewart: "BAAJA brought together the broadest and most diverse coalition of working interests that Washington has seen in decades who worked to pass a good piece of legislation that will let us build things in America again.

“It will ensure greater abundance and affordability for the next generation and we are proud to be a part of it.”

Western Energy Alliance: “We have a generational choice in front of us. We must decide if we’re going to be builders or not. If we’re going to meet our nation’s energy needs, or not. Reforming the nation’s outdated permitting system is critical to delivering affordable energy and growing jobs. Our nation’s economy can no longer sustain the strategy of activist groups to defer, delay, and deny high-value energy and infrastructure projects. This bill is an important step toward providing greater certainty, while still prioritizing the environment. It broadly benefits infrastructure development and all sources of energy production. We’re pleased to see senators come together in bipartisan manner to work out key differences for the benefit of the American people. We now urge lawmakers in the House to take the deal and deliver a win on energy affordability before the current session
ends.”

Distributed on November 20th, 2026.

Alabama Power is offering a rate reduction of about $160 million for 2027, starting with January bills.
Savings for residential customers
Savings depend on electricity use (compared with current rates at the same usage):
•  1,000 kWh/month (a common benchmark): more than $50 per year
•  750 kWh/month: about $40 per year
•  2,000 kWh/month: about $106 per year
The lower rate applies automatically to every monthly bill—no action is required from customers. Actual bills will still vary with usage and weather.
Why the decrease
The reduction is driven mainly by expected higher revenue in 2027 from large-load data centers. Alabama Power says these customers pay the full cost to serve them, which lowers the cost to serve other customers.
This announcement was made today (November 20, 2026) via a filing with the Alabama Public Service Commission. It follows an earlier commitment to freeze rates through 2027.

text:
Nick Saban says a former Alabama player who played pre-NIL told him getting paid $2,000,000 in college might have prevented him from becoming the man he became

“Who are you going to pay? What positions are most important? Because if you pay the wrong guys, and you’ve heard me say this before, you’re out of luck. When you can’t evaluate the players and you don’t pay the right guys, you’re going to pay the consequences for that in the future.”

“You’re going to spend all this money, you’re not going to have a very good team, and you’re not going to get the outcome everybody expects. And then the cause and effect of paying players is we’re raising money from alumni who now think they should have a say in what happens. And that’s why 33 coaches got fired last year, because of boosters. They have a say.”

“Look, talent is not talent if you can’t use it. So if you don’t have character to go with it, you probably can’t use it. And it’s not just in sports. Nobody who’s not really smart gets into medical school, but everybody doesn’t make it.”

“They’re talented enough, but they don’t make it. Some of them who make it don’t make very good doctors. So I always say talent is not talent if you can’t use it, which means you have to have some kind of competitive character to make the choices and decisions to create the habits. So you can recruit talent, but accountability and commitment you have to develop.”

“And most of the time you can develop it. So it’s going to be the coaches who can judge character, but then also have the ability to help their players create those things. Don’t let the money change you. Stay focused on the things you can control to develop value for your future, because there’s a lot more value out there.”

“But I will say one thing that’s very interesting to me. Former players who played for us, I’m not mentioning any names. They didn’t make the money, they didn’t get paid. They played, they created value, they made a lot of money in the NFL, and they played for a long time.”

“And one of them said to me the other day something that was kind of alarming. He said, ‘If I would have gotten paid $2 million when I played here, I don’t know if I would have become the man I became. I don’t know if I would have developed into the player I became. I don’t know that I wouldn’t have, but I don’t know if I could have handled that at 18 and 19 years old, and I don’t know if I would have become what I was able to become.’”

Axe Compute Q3 2026 Earnings: Revenue More Than Doubles

Axe Compute’s Q3 2026 results show how quickly the institutional demand for AI infrastructure is taking shape, and why its relationship with Aethir matters.

Revenue reached $7.2M, up 125% from $3.2M in Q2. 
All revenue came from GPU compute services, a clear signal that demand is moving beyond infrastructure promises into actual service delivery.

Net income came in at $11.5M, compared with a $17.2M loss in Q2. However, this figure included $10.5M in digital asset gains and a $4.6M non-cash unrealized gain. So, it’s important not to confuse reported net income with operating profitability.

The bigger story is the contract pipeline.

By September 29, Axe had signed contracts worth more than $3.45B, including over $2.8B from three July Build contracts across the US and Europe, plus a Georgia agreement worth more than $350M over five years.

These are contract values, not revenue already earned. Execution is now the real test.

In Georgia, Axe acquired a 2,304-unit NVIDIA B300 GPU cluster, comprising 288 Supermicro B300 NVL8 servers, with approximately 5MW of committed power. The $124.4M acquisition was provisioned by quarter-end, with customer acceptance still underway and commissioning expected between Q4 2026 and Q1 2027.

Another important metric: contract liabilities climbed to $569.3M, largely reflecting customer prepayments and deferred revenue. These prepayments help fund infrastructure deployment, although they also come with the responsibility to deliver the contracted compute.

This is where the Aethir connection becomes interesting.

@AethirCloud brings distributed GPU infrastructure and global compute capacity, while Axe provides an enterprise-facing commercial structure for large customers and contracts. Through initiatives like ACCELERATE, the relationship aims to expand institutional-grade GPU infrastructure across the US and Europe.

The takeaway? AI infrastructure is becoming a serious commercial market, and the competition is shifting from simply securing GPUs to delivering reliable compute at scale.

Axe CEO’s message captures the next phase perfectly: “Our job now is delivery.”

2026 has brought the contracts and the numbers. 2027 will show how much of that opportunity can become operational capacity and recognized revenue.

Assistant Property Manager - Birch Creek
Kent, WA · 21 hours ago

About the job

Job Summary

This position is open until filled; however, to ensure consideration applications should be submitted by December 7, 2026 at 4:30 p.m.

About

Are you looking for more than just a job? Looking for an opportunity to be passionate about what you do while providing resources to your community? Do you have great attention to detail and enjoy providing exceptional customer service? And are you someone that thrives in a fast-paced environment? If so, this position may be for you! King County Housing Authority is currently recruiting for an Assistant Property Manager to support our Birch Creek portfolio in Kent, Washington. The Assistant Property Manager will perform a variety of administrative duties related to the management of the Birch Creek portfolio. They will be responsible for ensuring that the property is operated in an efficient, cost-effective manner while providing high-quality, well-maintained housing for the residents and/or tenants. The successful candidate will be:

Interfacing with applicants, residents, vendors and neighbors.
Performing annual reviews and rent calculations for residents.

Providing front office face-to-face interactions with residents and partners.

Conducting annual inspections, lease-enforcement, and compiling data for use in reports.

Assisting with managing the operations as directed by the Property Manager.

King County Housing Authority (KCHA), an independent municipal organization is a high performing nationally recognized leader in affordable housing. To learn more about KCHA and our Mission visit this link.

We transform lives through housing.

Essential Functions

The Assistant Property Manager will:
Prepare and manage certification schedule; process all certification types for submission to the appropriate internal or external partnerships.
Manage, maintain, and execute records and files; sort, index, and file material according to company policy and procedures; destroy and delete files per company record retention schedule; handle administrative processes including purchasing, addressing accommodation and work order requests, aid on all other administrative needs as required.
Coordinate, develop, and consult executive and managerial staff providing system-wide comprehensive training programs; instruct and advise staff at every level of site management.
Receive tenant inquiries, complaints, and service requests and resolve them within the framework of established policies and procedures or forward them to appropriate party for disposition; prepare, post, and mail legal notices when violations occur.

Conduct unit and property inspections to ensure compliance with all program requirements.

Complete monthly financial narratives; prepare and analyze budget to ensure that property operates within budget restrictions.

Manage and monitor delinquency for all property tenant accounts; address issues as needed or required.

Create and manage a variety of legal notices to ensure that all residents maintain compliance with all lease restrictions; process evictions as requested or required.

Qualifications And Competencies

Required Qualifications:
Associate's degree AND
Moderate (1 to 3 years) experience in affordable housing, property management, fair housing, or general management OR
An equivalent combination of experience and education that provides the necessary knowledge, skills, and abilities to perform the essential functions of this position.
Required Knowledge, Skills, And Abilities
Demonstrated ability to prepare and maintain records (manual and electronic) and reports with a high level of accuracy and attention to detail; ability to perform mathematical calculations.
Knowledge of complex affordable housing programs including HUD rental assistance, LIHTC, HOME and/or other applicable regulated housing programs and Authority policies and procedures.
Strong organizational skills including prioritizing, ensuring accuracy, multi-tasking, and handling interruptions appropriately; ensures assignments are completed in a timely and effective manner.

Communicates effectively and collaboratively with individuals, and internal and external organizations; applies effective written and oral communication techniques to convey clear and timely messages.

Ability to work independently and as a team member to develop effective working relationships; works cooperatively, exchanges ideas, and addresses issues in a constructive, collaborative manner.

Adapts to changing business needs, conditions, and work responsibilities; responds to change with a positive attitude and a willingness to learn new ways to accomplish work activities and objectives.
Analyzes problems, identifies solutions, and articulates possibilities and recommendations; demonstrates critical, creative, and reflective thinking.
Utilizes excellent time management and problem-solving techniques, and use of professional judgment in complex situations; demonstrates strong project management skills.

Proficiency using MS Office applications including Word, Excel, Outlook and the Internet.

Ability to work effectively and positively with individuals of diverse cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds.
Special Requirements

Crazy catch-up for rest of the week + travel so late but folks liked the first so Day 2 notes from @TomorrowXSummit in Austin, plus a few wider observations across both days. They've uploaded almost all of these to YouTube so feel free to watch and make your own takeaways. Great to meet so many folks across the week!

Wider observations across both days:
>The clearest theme across both days was the split between operators on stage and investors in the hallways, who were effectively debating two different horizons: near-term physical demand and multi-year contract visibility versus capital intensity, financing costs, contract flexibility, and second-contract hardware economics.
>On stage across both days, @GavinSBaker repeatedly pressed operators on the same questions investors were debating off stage: whether demand shifted over the past month (Micron, Astera Labs), whether 27 years of broken semiconductor take-or-pay deals repeat in a 2029 downturn (Micron), whether enterprise AI spend grows or plateaus after open-weight routing (DoorDash), and how to underwrite commodity compute-resale risk, debt retirement, and cash burn (Fireworks AI, Cerebras, CoreWeave).
>Across the credit and capital markets sessions (Day 1's Apollo and Druckenmiller sessions alongside Day 2's Blackstone and AI Credit panels), funding-cost dispersion stood out, with ~700 bps separating OEM-backed chip loans from riskier long tail neo paper and lenders capping single-theme exposure.

Day 2 session notes (Wednesday, Nov 18)
>20 Watts: Lessons from SpaceX & Tesla (Antonio Gracias & Dr. Laura Harrison, PhD): Framed executive decision-making under stress around the brain's ~20W budget, using early SpaceX tests and Tesla's 2010 Fremont commitment as examples of keeping strategic options open rather than letting fear narrow the decision tree. @AntonioGracias 

>Blackstone (Jon Gray): Tested the bubble thesis across valuations (Nasdaq ~27x vs. >60x in 1999), constrained supply (portfolio AI spend up 20x), and leverage (hyperscalers near ~$1T EBITDA before capex/taxes next year). Highlighted ~7% AUM data-center exposure on 15–20 year leases to tenants averaging ~$2.5T market cap, DC site workers growing from 10k to 70k by end-2027, community compacts ($1.75B Indiana utility giveback, 5-year Iowa rate freeze, $105M Yellowstone gift), and lender concentration limits pushing more equity into large builds.

>Intel (Lip-Bu Tan): Disclosed Intel's first signed external 18A-P foundry customer (unnamed; 18A yields at 70%) and named Microsoft as its first public EMIB packaging customer alongside a multi-year Xeon (Diamond Rapids) supply deal. Targeted 14A internal volume in 2027 and external in 2028–29 (0.1 defect density target), sized server CPUs growing from $40B to $200B in 5 years, and called PCs the only soft demand pocket. @LipBuTan1

>Arm (Rene Haas): Moving beyond IP royalties (350B cumulative chips) to selling its own 136-core AGI CPU (target doubled from $1B to $2B, sold out) toward a ~$25B 4-year revenue goal (from ~$6B today). Noted his agents run 200–300 CPU cores simultaneously (vs. 8–16 on a laptop), pitched "same performance at half the power" vs. Intel, and warned U.S. data-center moratoriums push manufacturing abroad. @renehaas237

>DoorDash (Tony Xu): Defended the ~$17B ($65/sh) Instacart acquisition as lowering grocery fulfillment costs for independent grocers and noted DoorDash Dot completes ~10% of real orders in Phoenix. Shared that internal AI spend jumped 20x this year before plateauing via frontier efficiencies and fine-tuned open-weight routing (expecting spend to grow again as agentic tasks expand), while noting external agentic commerce is still "several hundred orders" total. @t_xu

>AI from the Credit Perspective (Scott Goodwin / Diameter & Andrew West / Oaktree): Goodwin sized financing needs at $3–5T (~40 GW/yr over 2 years), laid out a ~700 bps pricing ladder (7.5–8% Nvidia/Broadcom-backed 2.5-yr chip loans, 8.5% SpaceX secured, ~12% strong neocloud, 15%+ with warrants for riskier neolabs), and noted neoclouds need 30–40% more capital per GW than hyperscalers. West favored securitized/asset-backed structures (powered-shell bonds at 9–12% with IG offtake, neocloud converts at 50–70c, tenants prepaying 1–2 years of rent plus residual guarantees). @skgoodwin23

>The Boring Company (Steve Davis): Argued cheaper autonomous trips will increase surface traffic ("2D to 3D"), citing ~$5M/mile tunnel costs, 70 miles entitled for Vegas Loop (plus a 20-mile Nashville loop), and a Bastrop factory building >95% of boring-machine components in-house (~1 machine every 2 months).

>Micron (Sanjay Mehrotra & Dr. Scott DeBoer): Reported 75% of CY27 output sold out (CY27–28 tighter than 2026) across 26 multi-year SCAs ($32B in upfront cash and financial commitments) in a DRAM market consolidated from 10–15 players in 2000 to 3. Noted CHIPS Act buyback restrictions expire Dec 9 alongside >$250B in U.S. fabs, and stacked 3D DRAM reaches the market in 2028–29 (broad adoption 2030–31). @MicronCEO

>DigitalOcean (Paddy Srinivasan): Highlighted Q3 revenue of $321M (+40% YoY) with a >=60% FY27 outlook, $18M ARR per active MW across its entire fleet (90% of AI-customer revenue from accounts also using core cloud; 60% of revenue using 4+ products), ~700k paying customers (top 25 at 27% of Q3 revenue), 1.2x net leverage, and microVM sandboxes plus Action Gateway (20,000 tools) for agentic security. @paddix

>CoreWeave (Brannin McBee): Reported 81% of ~130k GPUs rolling off contract in 2027 have been re-leased through 2029 at higher ASPs (pointing to that cohort as validation of 6-year useful-life depreciation), >50% of new 2026 clients from enterprise, and 20–25% customer prepayments through 2027. Pressed on stage about using 2027 prepayments to retire ~15% unsecured debt ($47B Q3 debt), McBee framed it as a return trade-off against deploying more compute. @branninmcbee

>Atoms / CloudKitchens (Travis Kalanick): Runs ~500 properties targeting prepared, delivered meals at grocery-store cost (Pittsburgh food-robot factory opening Q1) and scaled Pronto autonomous mining to 2M-lb trucks running 35 mph at Brazil's Carajás iron-ore mine, alongside vocal public support for Jensen Huang. @travisk

>Perplexity (Aravind Srinivas): Grew revenue 4–5x on 10–20% headcount growth, expanding sales from 5 to 20–30 reps (30–60 day deal cycles across finance, legal, and corp dev). Pitched Perplexity Computer as a model-agnostic workflow layer charging token markup with low switching friction, targeting cash generation by late 2027 with 2028 as his base IPO mental model (2027 filing possible). @AravSrinivas

>Policy (David Sacks & Antonio Gracias): Expects post-midterm state data-center moratoriums and a federal AI-safety push. Supported codifying White House Accord transparency and audit provisions while strongly opposing a federal "Department of AI" pre-approving model releases, citing the Hugging Face sandbox-escape incident to argue for open-source security and Nvidia's role as the top U.S. open-source sponsor. @DavidSacks

>Cognition (Scott Wu): Crossed $1B ARR in under 2 years (expecting ~$1.6B end-January) with ~500 staff (~75 in eng/product/design). A 35% Devin Cloud price cut briefly dipped revenue before usage lifted it above the prior peak; launched Devin Bots for full-project ownership, runs 30–40% of tokens on post-trained open models (SWE-2 / SWE-2-Flash) at 5–10x lower cost, and flagged AI cyber defense as a major 2027 category. @ScottWu46

>Closing Keynote: SpaceX / xAI / Tesla (Elon Musk): Bringing on ~0.5 GW/month (~220k GB300s) now and targeting >1 GW/month by end-2027 (power-plant boundary) at ~60% of consensus capex. Rewrote xAI's training, RL, and inference stack in C/C++ (Grok 4.8 in RL), targeted a June 2027 Terafab test chip and late-2028 Phase 1 volume, and framed Starmind orbital solar AI satellites (200 GW/yr space solar manufacturing target) as the long-term scaling path. @elonmusk

EPISODE 3 — HILLARY RODHAM CLINTON: THE MACHINE'S OTHER HALF
A known socialist. [Allegedly.] 

Not a documented party member. 

Look at where she started, and look at what she built.

I. THE THESIS
1969, Wellesley College: her senior thesis, "There Is Only the Fight...": An Analysis of the Alinsky Model, a serious academic study of Saul Alinsky, the self-described radical organizer and author of Rules for Radicals. 

She interviewed him in Chicago and Boston, and invited him to Wellesley. 

In the thesis's own acknowledgments, she thanks "Mr. Alinsky for providing a topic, sharing his time and offering me a job." 

She confirmed it herself, decades later, in her memoir Living History: "He offered me the chance to work with him when I graduated from college, and he was disappointed that I decided instead to go to law school." 

She chose Yale instead. 

Her 1969 Wellesley commencement address, delivered as student body president, drew national press for its combative tone toward the establishment — enough that Life magazine covered it.

That's the starting point: not a woman who stumbled into activism, but one who studied its methods formally, as an undergraduate thesis, before she ever held office — and who said so herself, in her own book, years before anyone needed to dig it up.

II. THE EARLY INSTITUTIONS
Before politics, she worked at the Children's Defense Fund and the Legal Services Corporation in the 1970s — both federally-adjacent advocacy institutions built to expand legal and social services for the poor. 

Legitimate, well-documented work. 

Also the first visible step in a pattern: radical theory studied in college, then practiced through institutions respectable enough to carry it into the mainstream.

III. THE HEALTHCARE OVERHAUL
1993-94: she leads the administration's attempt to restructure the US healthcare system — the Health Security Act, which would have brought a large share of the private insurance market under federal coordination through regional purchasing alliances. 

It failed in Congress under the weight of its own complexity and industry opposition. 

It was, by scale, the most ambitious attempt at federal control of a major American industry since the New Deal — and it came from the First Lady's office, not a cabinet department.

IV. THE FOUNDATION
Before her 2009 confirmation as Secretary of State — confirmed 94-2 by the Senate, with only Republicans Jim DeMint and David Vitter voting no, a show of nearly unanimous bipartisan support — she agreed to submit any increase in foreign Clinton Foundation donations for State Department ethics review. 

An Associated Press investigation later found that at least 85 donors who'd given as much as $156 million met with her or sought her help while she ran State; the AP noted those meetings didn't appear to violate the ethics agreement itself. 

Real overlap. 
No established violation.

V. URANIUM ONE
2005: Bill Clinton and financier Frank Giustra fly to Kazakhstan, meeting its president around the time Giustra's company secures uranium rights there; Giustra donates $31+ million to the Clinton Foundation. 

2010: Russia's Rosatom moves to acquire a controlling stake in the successor company, Uranium One, a deal needing approval from CFIUS, a 9-agency panel that included the State Department she ran. 

Uranium One's chairman donates $2.35 million to the Foundation around the same period, undisclosed despite her 2009 pledge — a donation to the Foundation, not a payment to Hillary personally. 

Separately, Bill Clinton himself is paid $500,000 for a Moscow speech by a Russian bank simultaneously promoting Uranium One stock. 

CFIUS approved the deal that October. 

https://t.co/L7lcaTk7qp disputed the claim that she held personal veto power over the transaction — the approval came from the 9-agency panel as a body, not from her individually, though her department held one of the nine votes. 

What's undisputed is the size of the money, on both tracks, Foundation and personal, and the precision of its timing, again and again, around the same family.

VI. THE SERVER
She ran a private email server for official State Department business throughout her tenure — a setup first surfaced publicly by the House Select Committee on Benghazi, chaired by Republican Trey Gowdy of South Carolina, while investigating an unrelated matter. 

July 2016: 
FBI Director James Comey 

Not an activist socialist. [Allegedly].

announces no charges, but states plainly that Clinton and her colleagues were "extremely careless in their handling of very sensitive, highly classified information," and that evidence existed of potential statutory violations — just not enough, in his judgment, for any reasonable prosecutor to bring a case. 

Documented carelessness. 

No charge. 

That's the honest version, and it's damning enough without embellishment.

VII. BENGHAZI
September 11, 2012: 
The attack on the US diplomatic compound in Benghazi, Libya, under her State Department's watch, kills 4 Americans. 

The House Select Committee, Republican Trey Gowdy of South Carolina again!!
Spent over 2 years and $7 million on the investigation — the longest congressional probe in modern history — and found no new evidence contradicting the administration's account of the attack itself. 

That finding doesn't resolve the separate, earlier questions about security staffing and the warnings that preceded the attack, and it doesn't change that 4 Americans died. 

Those are different questions. 

The committee's answer to one isn't an answer to the other. 

(Fuller context on the attack itself sits in the Obama piece, since it happened on his watch too — this is her share of it.)

THE EMULSIFIER — THE CREDENTIAL
Bill's Emulsifier blended rival policies into one smooth center. 

Hers works differently: it takes something that started as genuinely radical — a 1969 thesis on Alinsky, a combative commencement speech, a job offer she herself confirmed accepting the compliment of, if not the job — and runs it through 50 years of credentialing. 

Yale Law. 

The Children's Defense Fund. 

First Lady. 
Senator. 
Secretary of State. 

Each institution is more respectable than the last, and each one launders a little more of the original edge out of the record, until what's left is a woman accused of being a radical by people who've never read the thesis, and defended as a pragmatist by people who've never asked why she wrote it, or why she still mentioned the job offer, fondly, in her own memoir decades later.

That's the Credential at work: not hiding the radicalism, but burying it under enough institutional legitimacy that asking about it starts to sound like the fringe position.

ETHOS
The same standard applies here as to her husband, and to Gowdy's committee, and to DeMint and Vitter's dissenting votes: look at what each investigation actually found, not at who ran it or why. 

A 2-year, $7 million inquiry that turns up a private server instead of the crime it was chasing is still worth taking seriously — just for what it actually found, not what it set out to prove. 

And a claim confirmed in the subject's own memoir needs no qualifier at all.

A known socialist. [Allegedly.] 

Not a documented party member. 

The thesis was real. 

So was the job offer. 

So was the credentialing that followed both.

She gave her intellect to an idea.
Evil collected the dividend.

THE ISLAND | Part 3 of 22

THE WARNINGS: Nine Years Before Anyone Acted

1996.A young artist named Maria Farmer contacts the FBI. She reports that Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell are sexually abusing minors.

Nine years later, Palm Beach police open the first real investigation.

In between, the warnings kept coming. 

So did the praise.

📘 THE CALL

The report. 

Farmer had worked for Epstein. 

The FBI's own record of her complaint, a report dated September 3, 1996, stayed hidden for nearly three decades. The Justice Department released it on December 19, 2025, under the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

What she said. 

According to House Oversight Democrats, she reported that Epstein and his associates were sexually abusing minors and producing child sexual abuse material.

What the FBI did. 

Not enough. 

Farmer's lawyers say the agent didn't follow up. In May 2025, she sued the federal government for negligence.

Who ran the FBI then? 1996 was the Clinton administration. Every administration after it inherited the same file.

🔍 THE PRAISE

October 2002. New York magazine profiles Epstein as an "International Moneyman of Mystery." Two very different men offer glowing quotes.

🔹 Donald Trump: "I've known Jeff for fifteen years. Terrific guy." And: "It is even said that he likes beautiful women as much as I do, and many of them are on the younger side."
🔹 Bill Clinton, through a spokesperson: "Jeffrey is both a highly successful financier and a committed philanthropist with a keen sense of global markets."

One article. A former Democratic president and a future Republican one. Both later said they knew nothing of his crimes.

🎯 THE STORY THAT GOT CUT

2003. Journalist Vicky Ward writes a Vanity Fair profile of Epstein. She says she had on-the-record accounts from a mother and her daughters. The oldest described Epstein trying to seduce her. Her younger sister was 16.

Ward's account. 

Her editor told her: "Graydon's taking out the women from the piece." She says she was told the editor-in-chief, Graydon Carter, was "sensitive about the young women."

The family. 

The sisters were Maria and Annie Farmer. Annie later testified under her own name at Ghislaine Maxwell's 2021 trial.

Carter's side. He denies the "sensitive" remark. He told Politico: "we didn't have confidence in Ward's reporting," and that she "didn't have the goods."

🕳️ THE PART YOU MISSED

The reviews that skipped it. 

In 2020, the Justice Department's ethics office reviewed how prosecutors handled Epstein in 2007-2008. It didn't examine the 1996 FBI complaint. In December 2025, Rep. Robert Garcia asked the Justice Department's inspector general to investigate both: the FBI's failure in the 1990s, and why later reviews never addressed it.

The math. 

1996 complaint. 2003 story cut. 2005 police investigation. 2008 deal. 2019 arrest. Twenty-three years from the first warning to federal charges.

🛡️ THEIR SIDE

Farmer's account of how the FBI handled her call comes from her lawsuit, not from an official finding. Carter stands by his editorial judgment. Trump says the two had a falling out years before Epstein's arrest, and Clinton says he knew "nothing" about Epstein's crimes. 

Neither has been accused of wrongdoing by prosecutors.

$KITE flipped long inside a weak 153-bar range. Kong Cloud scored the event at 11, in the Noise tier.

This is a useful case for understanding why a state change and structural confirmation are separate parts of the model.

The chart frame is a box from 0.0938 to 0.1536. It has four touches on one boundary and three on the other, spans 5.13 ATR, and lacks confirmation from the volume profile. KITE changed state at 0.1374, still inside that box. There was no event at either boundary.

In the Kong Cloud process, a ranging market routes through a structural classification before the score is assembled. The system asks whether price produced a breakout, breakdown, rejection, bounce, or remained inside the established range. Structure carries a weight of 35 in this regime because support and resistance define the frame while price is contained.

The crucial detail is that an established box is frozen. A close beyond a boundary can then be classified against a stable reference, consistent with the classical structural treatment associated with Edwards and Magee. Moving a boundary to accommodate each new close would erase the distinction between a contained move and an actual change in structure.

KITE produced the contained case. Its structural context was inside_range, which assigned a structural factor of zero. The structure component therefore added nothing to the score. This does not invalidate the long state. It says the state change has not received evidence from the part of the model with the largest ranging-regime weight.

The remaining evidence was limited. Volume measured 0.89 times its rolling 20-bar baseline and was declining. That sits in the normal 0.8 to 1.5 band, but the direction of volume offered no added confirmation. Momentum alignment was mixed. The five-day macro reading diverged.

Kong Cloud begins with smoothed state detection to reduce one-bar noise. It then requires three-bar confirmation before recording a flip. That answers one question: has the indicator state changed with enough persistence to count? The scoring layers answer a different question: how much independent evidence agrees with that change?

Separating those questions matters here. A flip can be genuine as an indicator event while remaining analytically weak as a Prime. The Kong Score of 11 records that distinction. It is a measured verdict on the available evidence, without forcing every detected change into a stronger narrative.

The next informative observation is structural. Persistence inside the box would leave the largest ranging component inactive. A close beyond 0.1536 or below 0.0938 would create a boundary event that can be evaluated on its own evidence, including volume behavior. text:
Alaska Shock: Senator Toppled By RCV Twist

https://t.co/ajb2A6JO3E
Alaska’s Senate flip turns on something more durable than one news cycle: how a ranked-choice system and a fractured Republican field met a coalition-ready Democrat with deep statewide roots—and produced a clear, rules-aligned win.
At a Glance

Democrat Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan for Alaska’s U.S. Senate seat, flipping it to Democrats.
Official Alaska Division of Elections tallies placed Peltola first in the statewide count; subsequent projections called the race for her.
Alaska’s ranked-choice system blunted any spoiler effect from similarly named candidates and reinforced Peltola’s advantage.
The outcome reflects Alaska’s post-2020 election architecture: open primaries, ranked-choice voting, and coalition-friendly politics.
What the results show and why they held
The decisive fact is straightforward: Democrat Mary Peltola finished ahead of two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in the statewide count, with the Alaska Division of Elections reporting Peltola at 141,637 votes (49.98%) to Sullivan’s 130,162 (45.93%), in a 283,377-vote contest. The margin—11,475 votes—made her the frontrunner heading into final tabulation and prompted major outlets to project the seat for Peltola, confirming one of the election’s most consequential flips in a state long considered right of center at the federal level.
Ranked-choice voting (RCV), now the backbone of Alaska’s general elections, mattered less as a late twist than as the structural context for the entire race. RCV requires a candidate to cross a majority threshold via sequential redistribution of lower-ranked choices if no one clears 50% on first preferences. In this contest, Peltola’s first-choice lead and the transfer patterns implied by public data meant that even if she finished a hair under 50% on first count, she was well-positioned to prevail on transfers—particularly given how nonmajor-party and similarly named candidates’ ballots tended to break.
Mechanics: how Alaska’s ranked-choice system shaped the outcome
Alaska adopted open primaries and RCV by ballot initiative in 2020; the state’s high court later upheld the framework, cementing it as the rule set for subsequent cycles. In practice, voters can rank multiple candidates, and if no one wins an outright majority in round one, the last-place finisher is eliminated and their votes are redistributed to the next-ranked candidate on each ballot; the process repeats until a candidate surpasses 50%.

Two dynamics in this Senate race rewarded coalition breadth over base intensity. First, a second “Dan Sullivan” (Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.) appeared on the ballot; his small share of first-choice votes raised tactical questions but did not eclipse Peltola’s lead when combined with the incumbent’s total. Second, analyses of Alaska’s prior RCV behavior and available election files indicated that a meaningful share of voters who selected the similarly named candidate also ranked Peltola second, a pattern that, under RCV, would tend to consolidate her advantage rather than spoil it. In other words, the system’s design absorbed potential confusion and converted it into transfers, not chaos.

The vote math: what was needed and what actually happened
Peltola’s first-choice share sat just at the cusp of a majority—effectively 50% on a 283,000-vote base—which is why projections were aggressive even before formal tabulation rounds were complete. The arithmetic favored her two ways. If late-counted ballots nudged her above 50%, she would win outright. If not, elimination rounds were likely to add to her total, not subtract from it, based on observed transfer behavior in earlier Alaska races and the specific mix of minor candidates in this field.

The incumbent’s path required either an improbable late surge from uncounted ballots concentrated in reliably Republican precincts or an unusually favorable transfer pattern from eliminated candidates’ ballots that overcame a five-figure deficit. Neither materialized at scale. Outlets subsequently called the race, and reporting from national and Alaska-focused desks aligned with the state’s data releases.

Why this flip was plausible in Alaska’s political ecosystem
The result is less an ideological whiplash than a lesson in how Alaska’s reengineered electoral incentives favor candidates who can harvest cross-partisan second choices. Peltola had already demonstrated that capacity in her 2022 special House victory, where she assembled a coalition that withstood late transfers from Republican-leaning voters. The 2026 Senate contest replayed that script: a Democrat with broad personal appeal and a reputation for Alaska-first pragmatism facing a divided Republican field under RCV rules that reward depth of support beyond first preferences.

That architecture also curbs classic spoiler risk. In a plurality system, a same-named challenger might split an incumbent’s base irretrievably. Under RCV, those ballots are not lost; if voters rank the incumbent second, their preferences flow back upon the challenger’s elimination. Where voters instead ranked Peltola second, the mechanism reflects actual voter intent—an argument for RCV’s resilience in the face of strategic candidacies and ballot-order idiosyncrasies documented by election scholars.

The “two Dan Sullivans” controversy and the rule of law
Late-campaign attention centered on allegations that Democrats recruited a similarly named candidate to siphon votes from the incumbent. Whatever the political theater, the legal and structural guardrails mattered more: the state’s RCV system mitigates misfire outcomes, the courts have affirmed Alaska’s authority to run its elections under this framework, and federal attempts to preemptively condition certification on a specific candidate’s victory were rejected as inconsistent with constitutional allocations of power to the states.

Put plainly, the system performed as designed. Voters could rank candidates; election officials followed statutory timelines for late-arriving absentee processing and tabulation; and when projections arrived, they reflected the combined effect of first-choice tallies and predictable transfer behavior under established law.

Consequences: what this means for governance and future campaigns
Peltola’s win expands Democrats’ Senate margin and gives Alaska a senator whose coalition was built as much on second-choice acceptability as first-choice fervor. That has implications for how she will govern—coalition-built winners tend to prize cross-aisle relationships—and for how challengers will campaign. Republican strategists in Alaska now face a strategic imperative: either consolidate the field before November or court second-choice rankings aggressively, because in an RCV regime, alienating adjacent blocs is a losing proposition even when base turnout is strong.

For reformers elsewhere, Alaska’s cycle offers two takeaways. First, RCV can reduce the payoff from cynical duplicate-name gambits or narrowcasting strategies that bank on plurality wins. Second, voter education remains essential. The system does not require a voter to rank multiple candidates, but ranking sincerely expands a ballot’s influence across rounds and more fully captures voter intent—an effect visible in the transfer math that underwrote Peltola’s advantage.
The bottom line
Mary Peltola’s ouster of a sitting Republican senator in Alaska is not a paradox; it is the anticipated product of a modernized election system meeting a candidate suited to it. The data from the state, the logic of ranked choice, and the projection calls point the same direction: a clear, rules-consistent result that turns a long-red seat blue and will shape how both parties approach Alaska for cycles to come.

Maryland’s Racing Commission has approved 114 live racing dates for Laurel Park and Pimlico in 2027, down from the 120 dates originally authorized for 2026.

The schedule reveals how much work remains in Maryland’s publicly financed effort to rebuild Pimlico and reshape the state’s horse racing industry.

▪️ TIMONIUM: Seven additional racing days are expected during the Maryland State Fair.

▪️ INDUSTRY PRESSURE: Churchill Downs and New York racing officials have created a new championship series excluding the Preakness, raising questions about Maryland’s position in national racing.

Maryland has committed substantial public resources to rebuilding Pimlico, but the transition to a year-round Baltimore racing facility remains unfinished.

The accountability questions: When will Pimlico accommodate its intended full racing schedule, and how will Maryland measure the economic return on its investment?

Delegates, Delegates, Delegates

The strongest delegate recruitment program begins with a county party Republicans know exists and want to be part of.

Too many Republicans have no idea their county party exists, who leads it, where it meets, or how to get involved. We will help counties become visible, accessible, and active in their communities so more Republicans know where to find us, how to join us, and why their involvement matters.

Too many county parties operate within the same small circle. Events draw the executive committee, an established faction, and the same familiar faces. Meanwhile, the broader Republican community remains disconnected from the organization that should be bringing them together.

We will help counties grow beyond that circle. That means reaching new people, welcoming them into the organization, building a committed team, and giving them meaningful opportunities to contribute. People should have a reason to come, a reason to return, and a reason to become part of the team.

Engagement comes first. Delegate recruitment follows.

Volunteers make strong delegates because they have already demonstrated commitment through their time and effort. We will help counties build a clear path from interested Republican to active volunteer to precinct delegate. As people get involved, understand the organization, and demonstrate commitment, we will encourage them to run.

The opening conversation should never be: “Here’s an affidavit. Fill it out, and your name will appear on the ballot.”

Yet too often, recruitment begins exactly there. Someone needs votes to control a county party or win a convention, so people are recruited to fill seats. They are told to attend a few meetings and vote, with little explanation of the role, little training, and little connection to the work of electing Republicans.

When recruitment revolves around an internal contest, we should not be surprised when factionalism and conflict follow. When people receive no preparation, support, or meaningful work, we should not be surprised when they disengage.

We will build a stronger foundation.

Grow the Republican community within each county. We will equip county parties with better outreach tools, useful data, and practical guidance to bring more Republicans into the organization. Events should welcome newcomers, create opportunities to connect, and lead to continued involvement. Every county should have a straightforward process for welcoming people, learning how they want to help, and following up.

Recruit through participation and commitment. We will encourage counties to develop future delegates through volunteer work and active involvement. People should understand the team they are joining and the mission they are helping advance before being asked to seek a position within it.

Set honest expectations upfront. Prospective delegates should understand the formal duties of the position and the active participation we expect from our team. Attending conventions matters. Helping elect Republicans matters. We will explain both clearly, without minimizing the commitment simply to get another name on the ballot.

Provide practical training and ongoing support. We will give counties a consistent onboarding framework covering party structure, delegate responsibilities, convention procedures, voter outreach, volunteer recruitment, and election activity. Every delegate should know where to start, whom to contact, and how to contribute.

Turn training into meaningful work. Delegates will have opportunities to welcome new volunteers, support events, contact voters, help candidates, and turn out Republicans. Counties will receive guidance for matching people with work that fits their abilities and availability. Participation should be purposeful, manageable, and connected to clear goals.

Measure engagement, not just filled seats. A full delegate roster means little if the people on it are disconnected from the organization. We will help counties track whether new members return, volunteers stay involved, delegates receive training, and participation grows. State party leadership will be accountable for providing resources that help counties make that progress.

Delegates are the backbone of the Michigan Republican Party. Building that backbone takes engagement, preparation, shared purpose, and sustained involvement.

Delegates deserve an organization that prepares them, supports them, and puts their commitment to work. County parties deserve more than a roster of names they hear from only at convention.

We will recruit for commitment, train for effectiveness, and organize to win elections.
